editor_spans.body: The full Motherwell speech partly answers the test we set last week, which was whether the offer to Holyrood would carry money and powers rather than warm words. The most substantive item is employment support. The Prime Minister offered 'DWP devolution', a localised model 'shaped by Holyrood', along with devolved innovation, enterprise and employability funding. These are things Westminster actually controls, so for once it is offering something it can give rather than telling Edinburgh what to give away.

There is a tension built into the offer. Powers would pass to Holyrood on the understanding that Holyrood then passes them further down to regions it is accused of starving. The speech calls Scotland 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe' and says the Scottish Government's own reform plan must 'move faster'. It also warns that Scottish towns could become 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up'. That is persuasion with pressure behind it. The real venue is the National Economic Council in a few weeks. It meets for the first time under this Prime Minister, and what matters is whether anything binding comes out of it.

The speech gets its history half right. Ravenscraig and the Leigh pits are fair examples of decisions taken far away by people who never lived with the consequences. But the deepest failure they describe is the absence of any transition plan: 'Nobody asked Leigh what was going to come next.' Regional power would not have kept a steelworks open against global markets. What it can do is make sure the next closure does not leave thirty years of empty land and empty high streets. Life-expectancy gaps of seven years across ten miles, and one in five shops empty in Dundee, are what decades without such plans look like.

The lever most fully in the Prime Minister's own hands gets the least detail. As mayor, he paid a premium so that Greater Manchester's buses were built in Falkirk, and he now says all UK public procurement should 'work like that'. Changing Whitehall's habit of buying the cheapest contract anywhere in the world needs no agreement from Holyrood. It would do more for reindustrialisation than the £10 million matched for defence colleges. Ministers should be judged on whether procurement rules actually change.

The one-in-six figure for young people not in education, employment or training is the number that ties this speech to the long story of deindustrialised places. The 'Easterhouse principle' of names not numbers is a sound idea. But it took a voluntary project on one estate years to build trust, and turning it into national employment policy risks producing the top-down scheme the speech itself condemns.
